What is Android: Android is a mobile operating system based on a modified version of the Linux kernel and other open-source software, designed primarily for touchscreen mobile devices such as smartphones and tablets. Developed by Google, Android is the world's most widely used mobile OS, powering billions of devices worldwide.
Kotlin Syntax & Conventions: Kotlin is a modern JVM language with concise syntax, null safety, and full Java interop. It eliminates boilerplate like getters/setters and semicolons. Android Studio provides first-class Kotlin support with automatic Java-to-Kotlin conversion.
Object-Oriented Kotlin: Kotlin classes use concise syntax with primary constructor, `init` blocks, and `data class` for value objects. Properties auto-generate getters/setters. Use `object` for singletons and `companion object` for static members.
Java Interop: Kotlin compiles to JVM bytecode and interoperates seamlessly with Java. Use `@JvmStatic`, `@JvmName`, and `@JvmOverloads` annotations to adjust Kotlin declarations for Java callers. Nullability is expressed with `@Nullable`/`@NonNull` platform types.
Collections & Lambdas: Kotlin's standard library provides rich collection operations: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `groupBy`, and more. Lambdas use `{ it -> }` syntax. Sequences (`asSequence()`) enable lazy evaluation for large collections.
Null Safety: Kotlin eliminates null pointer exceptions through its type system. Types are non-nullable by default. Use `?` for nullable types, `?.` for safe calls, `?:` for elvis operator, and `!!` only when you're sure the value isn't null.
Extension Functions: Extension functions add new behavior to existing classes without inheritance. They're resolved statically (compile-time polymorphism). Kotlin stdlib uses extensions extensively (e.g., `Context.toast()` patterns in Android).
Sealed & Data Classes: Sealed classes define restricted class hierarchies — all subclasses are known at compile time. They're ideal for representing states (Loading/Success/Error). Data classes auto-generate `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy`, and destructuring operators.

Activities & Lifecycle: An Activity is a single focused screen. The lifecycle includes `onCreate`, `onStart`, `onResume`, `onPause`, `onStop`, `onDestroy`. Use `Lifecycle`/`LiveData` to react to lifecycle changes. Avoid doing long work in `onPause`/`onStop`.
Services: Services run background operations without a UI. Foreground Services show a persistent notification. Use `JobIntentService` for backwards-compatible background work. Android 8+ limits background start; use `startForegroundService()` for immediate work.
Broadcast Receivers: Broadcast Receivers respond to system-wide events (e.g., connectivity change, boot complete). Declare in manifest or register dynamically. Android 8+ restricts implicit broadcasts — use `registerReceiver` for explicit or contextual broadcasts.
Content Providers: Content Providers manage shared app data with a URI-based interface. They enable secure data sharing between apps. Use `CP` for structured access to SQLite, file storage, or cloud data. `ContentResolver` queries providers from other apps.
Intents & Intent Filters: Intents are messaging objects for component communication: explicit (specific class) or implicit (action + data). Intent Filters declare what implicit intents a component can handle. `Intent.ACTION_VIEW`, `ACTION_SEND`, and custom actions are common.
Manifest & Permissions: AndroidManifest.xml declares app components, permissions, features, and metadata. Permissions are categorized: Normal (auto-granted), Dangerous (runtime request), Signature (same signing key). Android 11+ has package visibility and scoped storage changes.

<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.INTERNET" />       <!-- Normal -->
<uses-permission android:name="android.permission.ACCESS_FINE_LOCATION" /> <!-- Dangerous -->

<!-- Request dangerous permission at runtime -->
if (ContextCompat.checkSelfPermission(this, Manifest.permission.CAMERA)
    != PackageManager.PERMISSION_GRANTED) {
    ActivityCompat.requestPermissions(this, arrayOf(Manifest.permission.CAMERA), REQ_CAMERA)
}

<uses-feature android:name="android.hardware.camera" android:required="false" />
App Resources: Android resource system separates code from assets: layouts, strings, drawables, colors, dimensions, and themes. Use `res/` directories with qualifiers for density (`mdpi`/`hdpi`/`xhdpi`), locale, configuration. String resources enable localization without code changes.

<!-- res/values/strings.xml -->
<resources>
    <string name="app_name">MyApp</string>
    <string name="welcome">Welcome, %s!</string>
</resources>

<!-- res/values-es/strings.xml (Spanish) -->
<resources>
    <string name="welcome">¡Bienvenido, %s!</string>
</resources>

// In code
val msg = getString(R.string.welcome, username)

// Resource qualifier priority: locale > layout direction > smallestWidth > density > API level

ConstraintLayout & Views: ConstraintLayout is the default Android layout — build flat, flexible UIs with constraints between siblings and parent. Use `layout_constraint*` attributes for positioning. `Guideline`, `Barrier`, `Group`, and `Flow` are helper constructs for complex layouts.

<androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout
    android:layout_width="match_parent" android:layout_height="match_parent">

    <Button android:id="@+id/btn"
        app:layout_constraintTop_toTopOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintStart_toStartOf="parent"
        app:layout_constraintEnd_toEndOf="parent"
        android:text="Center" />

    <androidx.constraintlayout.widget.Guideline
        android:id="@+id/guide" android:orientation="horizontal"
        app:layout_constraintGuide_percent="0.5" />
</androidx.constraintlayout.widget.ConstraintLayout>
RecyclerView & Adapters: RecyclerView efficiently displays large lists by recycling item views. Use `ListAdapter` with `DiffUtil` for automatic, animated updates. `ConcatAdapter` merges multiple adapter types (header + list + footer). `ItemTouchHelper` enables swipe-to-dismiss and drag-and-drop.
Jetpack Compose Basics: Jetpack Compose is Android's declarative UI toolkit. Composable functions define UI as a function of state. No XML layouts — everything is Kotlin. `remember`, `mutableStateOf`, and `LaunchedEffect` manage state and side effects. Preview annotations render in IDE.
Compose State & Side Effects: State in Compose is observed automatically. `remember` retains state across recompositions. `LaunchedEffect` runs coroutines in composition scope. `DisposableEffect` handles cleanup. `derivedStateOf` computes derived state efficiently. Avoid triggering recompositions unnecessarily.
Navigation Component: Navigation Component handles fragment/destination transitions, back stack, deep links, and type-safe argument passing. Define navigation graph as XML or in Compose. `NavHost` + `composable()` routes power Compose Navigation. Pass args via `navArgument` or serializable types.
Material Design 3: Material Design 3 (Material You) provides dynamic theming based on wallpaper colors on Android 12+. Components include `NavigationBar`, `TopAppBar`, `FloatingActionButton`, `Card`, `BottomSheet`, `Snackbar`, `Modal`. Use `MaterialTheme.colorScheme` for adaptive colors.
Custom Views & Canvas: Custom Views extend `View` and override `onDraw(canvas: Canvas)` for pixel-level rendering. `Canvas` provides draw methods (circle, rect, path, bitmap, text). `Paint` controls style, color, stroke, and effects. Use `invalidate()` to trigger redraw. Prefer Compose Canvas for new work.

MVVM & ViewModel: ViewModel holds UI state and survives configuration changes (rotation). MVVM pattern: View observes ViewModel state via LiveData or StateFlow. ViewModel interacts with Repository (data layer). Never pass Context to ViewModel — use `AndroidViewModel` only when necessary.
LiveData & StateFlow: LiveData is lifecycle-aware, observation-based data holder. StateFlow is the Kotlin-idiomatic alternative with `Flow` operators, no lifecycle awareness (use `repeatOnLifecycle`), and doesn't auto-dispose. For new code, prefer `StateFlow` + `collectAsState()` in Compose.
Repository Pattern: Repository abstracts data sources (network vs cache vs database). The ViewModel calls repository methods without knowing where data comes from. Offline-first: save to local database first, sync to remote. `Flow<Resource<T>>` pattern handles Loading/Success/Error states.
Dependency Injection (Hilt): Hilt simplifies Dagger DI for Android with annotation-based setup. `@HiltAndroidApp` on Application, `@AndroidEntryPoint` on Activities/Fragments, `@HiltViewModel` on ViewModels. `@Module` + `@Provides` for third-party objects. `@Singleton` for app-scoped instances.
Clean Architecture: Clean Architecture layers: `domain` (entities + use cases + repository interfaces), `data` (repository implementations + DTOs + data sources), `presentation` (ViewModels + UI). Dependencies point inward — outer layers depend on inner layers, never vice versa.
WorkManager: WorkManager schedules deferrable, guaranteed background work that survives app restart and device reboot. Supports one-time (`OneTimeWorkRequest`) and periodic (`PeriodicWorkRequest`) tasks. Chain workers with `beginWith()` / `then()`. Constraints: network, battery, idle.

Retrofit & OkHttp: Retrofit turns HTTP API into a type-safe Kotlin interface. OkHttp handles low-level requests, connection pooling, and interceptors (logging, auth headers, caching). Use `suspend` functions for coroutine support. Add `HttpLoggingInterceptor` for debugging.
Room Database: Room is Android's ORM over SQLite. Define entities with `@Entity`, DAOs with `@Dao`. Use `@Query` for custom SQL. Room supports `Flow` return types for reactive queries. Migrations handle schema changes. `@ForeignKey` defines relationships.
DataStore & SharedPreferences: DataStore replaces SharedPreferences with coroutine-based, type-safe storage. `Preferences DataStore` for simple key-value, `Proto DataStore` for typed objects with schema. DataStore runs on `Dispatchers.IO` and handles data consistency. Never use SP in new code.
File Storage & Scoped Storage: Android 10+ uses Scoped Storage — apps can't randomly access the filesystem. Use `MediaStore` for shared media, `SAF` (Storage Access Framework) via `ACTION_OPEN_DOCUMENT` for user-selected files. App-specific storage (`getFilesDir()`, `getCacheDir()`) doesn't need permissions.
Firebase Integration: Firebase provides backend services: Authentication, Firestore (NoSQL DB), Realtime Database, Cloud Functions, Storage, Crashlytics, Analytics, Remote Config. Use `FirebaseApp.initializeApp()` once. Firestore queries are real-time via snapshot listeners or `get()` one-shot.
GraphQL (Apollo): Apollo GraphQL generates type-safe Kotlin client from `.graphql` queries. Define operations in `.graphql` files, Apollo generates data classes. Supports caching, pagination (`@connection`), subscriptions via WebSocket. Use `apolloClient.query()` / `.mutation()`.
WebSockets: WebSockets maintain persistent connections for real-time communication. OkHttp provides WebSocket support out of the box. Use `WebSocketListener` for events. For higher-level abstractions, use `Ktor` client WebSocket. Pair with `StateFlow` for reactive UI updates.

Coroutines & Flow: Coroutines are Kotlin's structured concurrency framework. `launch` for fire-and-forget, `async/await` for parallel work, `withContext` to switch dispatchers. `Flow` emits multiple values over time. Use `flow { }` builder, `catch`, `retry`, `combine`, and `flatMapLatest` operators.
Dispatchers & Contexts: Dispatchers define thread pools: `Dispatchers.Main` (UI thread), `IO` (network/disk), `Default` (CPU work), `Unconfined` (not recommended). `newSingleThreadContext()` for isolated work. Use `CoroutineExceptionHandler` for uncaught exceptions. Structured concurrency ensures child coroutines complete before parent.
Channels & Concurrency: Channels pass values between coroutines (producer-consumer). `Channel<T>` with `send()` / `receive()`. `produce { }` builder creates `ReceiveChannel`. Use `BroadcastChannel` (deprecated) or `SharedFlow` for one-to-many. `Mutex` and `Semaphore` protect shared resources.
RxJava (Observables): RxJava provides Observable streams with rich operators (map, filter, flatMap, debounce, retry, combineLatest). Use `Single` (1 emission), `Maybe` (0-1), `Completable` (completion signal). `Schedulers.io()`, `computation()`, `mainThread()`. Most new code uses coroutines, but legacy codebases use RxJava.
ExecutorService: For low-level threading, `ExecutorService` manages thread pools. Android provides `AsyncTask` (deprecated). Prefer coroutines, but understand executors for legacy code and custom thread pools. `Executors.newFixedThreadPool()`, `newCachedThreadPool()`, `ScheduledExecutorService`.
ANR & Threading: Application Not Responding (ANR) occurs when the main thread is blocked for >5 seconds. Causes: disk I/O, network calls, DB queries, `Thread.sleep()` on main thread. Use `StrictMode` to detect accidental main-thread work during development. Profile with Android Studio CPU profiler.

JUnit & Mockito: JUnit 5 is the standard unit testing framework. Mockito mocks dependencies. Use `@Test`, `@Before`, `@After`. `verify()` checks interactions. `when()` stubs return values. Use `ArgumentCaptor` for callback arguments. Run in `test/` directory (not `androidTest/`).
Espresso & UI Tests: Espresso tests UI interactions on real devices/emulators. `onView(withId(R.id.btn)).perform(click())`. Use `withText()`, `isDisplayed()`, `hasErrorText()`. `IdlingResource` waits for async work. `ActivityScenario` manages activity lifecycle. Run in `androidTest/` directory.
Compose Testing: Compose tests use `ComposeTestRule` and `onNodeWithText` / `onNodeWithTag` semantics matchers. `performClick()`, `performTextInput()`, `performScrollTo()`. Use `semantics { }` to add test tags. `useUnmergedTree = true` for testing inside merged nodes.
ADB & Logcat: ADB (Android Debug Bridge) is the universal command-line tool for device communication. Logcat filters system and app logs. Use `Log.v()`, `Log.d()`, `Log.i()`, `Log.w()`, `Log.e()` with consistent tags. `adb shell` for device shell access. `adb bugreport` dumps device state.

// Logging
private const val TAG = "NoteFragment"
Log.d(TAG, "Loading note ${noteId}")
Log.e(TAG, "Failed to load", exception)

// ADB commands
$ adb devices                           # list devices
$ adb logcat -s NoteFragment:D          # filter by tag + level
$ adb logcat -v threadtime NoteFragment:V *:S  # verbose custom tag, silent rest
$ adb shell am force-stop com.example.app    # kill app
$ adb shell dumpsys meminfo com.example.app   # memory info
$ adb exec-out screencap -p > screen.png      # screenshot
Profiler & Memory Leaks: Android Studio Profiler tracks CPU, memory, network, and energy. Memory Profiler detects leaks via heap dumps and reference trees. Common leaks: static references to Activity, inner classes holding outer references, unregistered listeners, Handler posts, retained Fragments.
CI/CD with GitHub Actions: Automate Android build, test, and deployment with GitHub Actions. Cache Gradle dependencies for faster builds. Use `actions/upload-artifact` for APK/AAB. `google-github-actions/submit` uploads to Play Console. `danger` for PR checks. `lint` + `ktlint` enforce code quality.

name: Android CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with:
          distribution: 'temurin'
          java-version: '17'
      - uses: gradle/actions/setup-gradle@v3
      - run: ./gradlew lint test assembleDebug
      - uses: actions/upload-artifact@v4
        with:
          name: apk
          path: app/build/outputs/apk/debug/*.apk
      - name: Submit to Play Console
        if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
        uses: google-github-actions/submit@v1

App Signing & Play Console: Google Play requires app signing. Play App Signing manages the signing key (Google stores your key securely). Use `jks` or `keystore` for upload key. Configure signing in `build.gradle.kts`. `app-signing` tool generates the key. Never commit keystore files to VCS.
App Bundle & APK: Android App Bundle (AAB) is the preferred publishing format — Google Play generates optimized APKs per device configuration (density, ABI, language). APKs are for direct installation. Use `./gradlew bundleRelease` for AAB, `assembleRelease` for APK. AAB reduces download size by ~35% on average.
ProGuard & R8: R8 shrinks, obfuscates, and optimizes code. ProGuard rules define what to keep (e.g., data classes for serialization, reflection targets, JNI methods). Enable with `isMinifyEnabled = true`. `consumer-rules.pro` for library consumers. Use `-printusage` to find dead code.
In-App Purchases: Google Play Billing Library handles in-app purchases and subscriptions. Products are managed in Play Console. Use `BillingClient` for querying, purchasing, and acknowledging purchases. Server-side validation (via Play Developer API) is recommended for security. `BillingFlowParams` launches purchase UI.
Push Notifications: Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) delivers push notifications. `FirebaseMessagingService` handles incoming messages. Notification channels (Android 8+) categorize notification types. Display notifications via `NotificationCompat.Builder`. Handle data payloads in `onMessageReceived`.

<service android:name=".MyFcmService" android:exported="false">
    <intent-filter>
        <action android:name="com.google.firebase.MESSAGING_EVENT" />
    </intent-filter>
</service>

class MyFcmService : FirebaseMessagingService() {
    override fun onMessageReceived(message: RemoteMessage) {
        val channelId = "notes_channel"
        val channel = NotificationChannel(channelId, "Notes", NotificationManager.IMPORTANCE_HIGH)
        getSystemService<NotificationManager>()?.createNotificationChannel(channel)

        val notification = NotificationCompat.Builder(this, channelId)
            .setSmallIcon(R.drawable.ic_note)
            .setContentTitle(message.notification?.title ?: "New note")
            .setContentText(message.notification?.body)
            .setAutoCancel(true)
            .build()
        NotificationManagerCompat.from(this).notify(1001, notification)
    }

    override fun onNewToken(token: String) {
        // Send token to server
    }
}

What is iOS: iOS is a mobile operating system created and developed by Apple Inc. exclusively for its hardware. It powers iPhone, iPad, and iPod Touch devices. Known for its smooth performance, security, and ecosystem integration, iOS is the second most popular mobile OS worldwide.
Swift Basics & Optionals: Swift is a type-safe, compiled language with optionals, value semantics, and protocol-oriented design. `let` for constants, `var` for variables. Optionals (`Type?`) safely represent absence. Use `if let` / `guard let` for unwrapping. `??` is the nil-coalescing operator.
Structs & Classes: Structs are value types (copied on assignment), classes are reference types (shared reference). Swift encourages structs for data models — they have automatic memberwise initializers and are thread-safe. Classes support inheritance and deinitializers. `mutating` keyword for struct methods that modify properties.
Protocols & Extensions: Protocols define interfaces that types can adopt. Extensions add functionality to existing types (including system types). Protocol extensions provide default implementations. `Equatable`, `Hashable`, `Codable`, `Comparable` are standard library protocols. Protocol-oriented programming is a Swift paradigm.
Generics & Error Handling: Generics enable type-parameterized functions and types. Swift uses `throws`/`try`/`catch` for errors, `Result<Success, Failure>` for completion handlers. Custom errors conform to `Error` enum or struct. `defer` guarantees cleanup code runs on scope exit.
Closures & Higher-Order: Closures are self-contained function blocks. They capture and store references to variables from their surrounding context. Higher-order functions: `map`, `filter`, `reduce`, `compactMap`, `flatMap`, `sorted`, `forEach`. Trailing closure syntax places closures outside parentheses.
Objective-C Interop: Swift and Objective-C can coexist in the same project via bridging header (`Project-Bridging-Header.h`). Swift classes marked `@objc` are visible to ObjC. ObjC categories become Swift extensions. Use `#import "ProductModuleName-Swift.h"` in ObjC to use Swift classes. Nullability annotations improve Swift interface.
Swift Concurrency (async/await): Swift 5.5+ introduces structured concurrency with `async`/`await`, `Task`, and `TaskGroup`. `async` marks a function as asynchronous. `await` suspends execution until the async function completes. `Task` creates a new async context. `TaskGroup` runs parallel child tasks.

Xcode IDE & Shortcuts: Xcode is the official IDE for Apple platforms. Key shortcuts: `Cmd+B` (build), `Cmd+R` (run), `Cmd+U` (test), `Cmd+Shift+K` (clean), `Cmd+0` (navigator toggle), `Cmd+Shift+Y` (debug area). `Ctrl+6` jumps to symbol. Use behaviors for automated workspace setup. Simulator `Cmd+Shift+H` for home.
Project & Target Configuration: Xcode projects have multiple targets (app, extensions, watch, tests). Build settings include code signing, deployment target, Swift language version, and build phases. `Info.plist` declares app capabilities and permissions. Schemes define build+run+test+profile configurations.
Storyboards & XIBs: Storyboards define app flow with segues and scenes. XIBs (nibs) are single-view reusable files. Segues can be show, present, or custom. `UIStoryboardSegue` subclass for custom transitions. While UIKit remains relevant, SwiftUI is Apple's recommended approach for new apps.
MVC, MVVM, VIPER: MVC (Model-View-Controller) is Apple's default pattern but leads to Massive View Controllers. MVVM adds a ViewModel with data binding via Combine/ObservableObject. VIPER (View-Interactor-Presenter-Entity-Router) provides strict separation for large apps. SwiftUI encourages MVVM with `@Observable`.
Coordinator Pattern: Coordinator pattern removes navigation logic from ViewControllers. Each coordinator owns its navigation flow. Child coordinators handle sub-flows. `UINavigationControllerDelegate` coordinates transitions. This pattern prevents Massive View Controller syndrome and enables deep linking.
Swift Packages & SPM: Swift Package Manager (SPM) is Apple's dependency manager integrated into Xcode. `Package.swift` declares dependencies and targets. Packages can be libraries, executables, or system modules. Xcode >File >Add Package Dependencies. SPM is preferred over CocoaPods/Carthage for new projects.

UITableView & UICollectionView: UITableView presents a single-column list with optional sections. UICollectionView offers flexible multi-column layouts. Both use `DataSource` and `Delegate` patterns. `UITableViewDiffableDataSource` simplifies snapshot-based updates with automatic animations. Self-sizing cells use Auto Layout constraints.
Auto Layout & Constraints: Auto Layout defines UI positions via constraints relative to sibling/parent views. Use `NSLayoutConstraint.activate()` for programmatic layout. `UILayoutGuide` creates spacer views. `UIStackView` simplifies sequential layouts. Safe area insets account for notch/Dynamic Island.
SwiftUI Views & Modifiers: SwiftUI uses declarative `View` building blocks. `VStack`, `HStack`, `ZStack` for layout. Modifiers (.padding(), .background(), .font()) configure views. `@ViewBuilder` for conditional content. `ForEach` for lists. `resizable`, `aspectRatio`, `scaledToFill/Fit` for images.
SwiftUI State Management: State property wrappers: `@State` (local view state), `@Binding` (passed reference), `@StateObject` (owned ObservableObject), `@ObservedObject` (passed reference object), `@EnvironmentObject` (shared via environment), `@AppStorage` (UserDefaults wrapper). `@Observable` macro (iOS 17+) simplifies observation.
Navigation & Tab Bars: SwiftUI: `NavigationStack` (push navigation), `TabView` (bottom tabs), `.sheet()` (modal), `.fullScreenCover()`. UIKit: `UINavigationController`, `UITabBarController`. Tab bars contain navigation controllers. `NavigationLink` in SwiftUI pushes destinations. `TabView` with `selection` binding for programmatic tab switching.
Animations & Transitions: SwiftUI provides implicit (`.animation()`) and explicit (`withAnimation`) animations. Transitions control how views enter/exit (`.opacity`, `.move`, `.slide`, `.scale`). `matchedGeometryEffect` animates between views. In UIKit, `UIView.animate(withDuration:)` and `UIViewPropertyAnimator` handle animations.
Swift Charts: Swift Charts (iOS 16+) provides declarative charting integrated with SwiftUI. `Chart { }` with `BarMark`, `LineMark`, `AreaMark`, `PointMark`, `RuleMark`. Customize with `.foregroundStyle`, `.annotation`, `.chartXScale`, `.chartYAxis` and interactive `chartGesture`.

ViewController Lifecycle: UIViewController lifecycle: `loadView`, `viewDidLoad`, `viewWillAppear`, `viewDidAppear`, `viewWillDisappear`, `viewDidDisappear`. `viewDidLoad` fires once. Use `viewWillAppear` for repeated UI updates. `deinit` for cleanup. SwiftUI uses `.onAppear`/`.onDisappear` modifiers.
UINavigationController: UINavigationController manages a stack of view controllers with a navigation bar. Push via `pushViewController(_:animated:)`, pop via `popViewController(animated:)`. Navigation bar can show title, left/right bar buttons, and a back button. `UINavigationBarAppearance` customizes navigation bar appearance globally.
TabBarController: UITabBarController switches between view controllers via bottom tabs. Each tab typically wraps a UINavigationController. Tab bar items have title, image, selected image, and badge. `UITabBarAppearance` for customization. SwiftUI's `TabView` provides equivalent functionality.
Alert & ActionSheet: UIAlertController presents alerts (modal) and action sheets (bottom). Alerts have text fields, confirm/cancel buttons. Action sheets present multiple destructive/neutral/cancel options. In SwiftUI, use `.alert()` and `.confirmationDialog()` modifiers.
Search & UserDefaults: UISearchController integrates search into navigation bars. `UISearchResultsUpdating` for real-time filtering. `UISearchBarDelegate` for search actions. `UserDefaults` stores small key-value data. SwiftUI provides `.searchable()` modifier and `@AppStorage` property wrapper.
Notifications (Push & Local): UNUserNotificationCenter handles local and push notifications. Request authorization with `.requestAuthorization()`. Create `UNNotificationContent` with title, body, sound, badge. `UNCalendarNotificationTrigger` for date-based, `UNTimeIntervalNotificationTrigger` for interval-based, `UNPushNotificationTrigger` for remote.

URLSession & Networking: URLSession performs HTTP requests. `URLSession.shared` for simple requests, custom sessions with configuration for advanced use. `dataTask(with:)` for raw data, `downloadTask` for files. Async/await wrappers simplify completion handler patterns. Supports caching, cookies, and background transfers.
Codable & JSON: Codable (Encodable & Decodable) provides automatic JSON serialization for Swift types. `JSONEncoder` and `JSONDecoder` handle conversion. Custom keys via `CodingKeys` enum. `snake_case` decoding strategy handles API conventions. Nested containers extract deeply nested data.
CoreData & CloudKit: CoreData is Apple's object graph and persistence framework. `NSPersistentContainer` manages the stack. `NSManagedObject` subclasses represent entities. `@FetchRequest` in SwiftUI auto-updates views. CloudKit syncs CoreData across devices with `NSPersistentCloudKitContainer`. Use `NSFetchedResultsController` for UIKit.
SwiftData: SwiftData (iOS 17+) is Apple's modern persistence framework built on Swift macros. `@Model` macro marks persistable classes. `@Query` fetches data reactively. `modelContainer` provides storage. `ModelContext` handles CRUD. SwiftData replaces CoreData for new apps targeting iOS 17+.
FileManager & Documents: FileManager handles file system operations: create, read, write, delete, move. Sandbox directories: `Documents/` (user data, backed up), `Library/Caches/` (temp files, not backed up), `tmp/` (temporary). iOS uses sandboxing — each app has its own container. Use `NSFileCoordinator` for coordinated access.
WebSockets & Combine: URLSessionWebSocketTask provides WebSocket support in iOS 13+. Combine is Apple's reactive framework: `Publisher`, `Subscriber`, `Operator`. Use `PassthroughSubject` for imperative-to-reactive bridging. Foundation publishers: `URLSession.dataTaskPublisher`, `NotificationCenter.Publisher`, `Timer.publish`.

GCD & OperationQueue: Grand Central Dispatch manages thread pools. `DispatchQueue.main.async` for UI work, `DispatchQueue.global(qos:)` for background. `DispatchGroup` synchronizes multiple tasks. `DispatchWorkItem` allows cancellation. `OperationQueue` adds dependency management and KVO. Prefer Swift async/await for new code.
async/await & Task: Swift structured concurrency: `Task` creates async context, `Task.detached` for unrelated work. `TaskGroup` for dynamic parallelism. `Task.yield()` for cooperative cancellation checks. `MainActor` ensures UI-thread execution. `@MainActor` attribute on types or functions guarantees main-thread dispatch.
Actors & Sendable: Actors protect mutable state from data races. All actor properties are isolated to the actor. `Sendable` protocol guarantees type-safe cross-concurrency passing. `@MainActor` is a global actor for UI thread. `nonisolated` for synchronous access to actor constants. `executor` for custom serial queues.
ARC & Memory Management: Automatic Reference Counting (ARC) tracks strong references. When count reaches zero, memory is deallocated. Strong reference cycles (retain cycles) cause leaks. Use `weak` (becomes nil) or `unowned` (never nil, crashes if deallocated) to break cycles. `Capture list` (`[weak self]`) in closures prevents cycles.
Weak/Strong References: Weak references don't increase reference count and automatically become `nil` when the object deallocates. Unowned references assume the object never deallocates during use (crashes if deallocated). In closures, `[weak self]` creates an optional, `[unowned self]` creates a non-optional. Prefer `weak` unless you're certain.

XCTest & XCTestExpectation: XCTest is Apple's testing framework. `XCTestCase` subclasses contain test methods starting with `test`. `XCTAssert*` functions verify conditions. `XCTestExpectation` waits for async work: `fulfill()` completes expectations, `wait(for:timeout:)` blocks until fulfillment. `measure { }` benchmarks performance.
UI Tests & XCUITest: XCUITest automates UI interactions. `XCUIApplication` launches the app. Query elements by type, identifier, label, or predicate. `tap()`, `typeText()`, `swipeUp()`, `press(forDuration:)`. `waitForExistence(timeout:)` for async UI. Accessibility identifiers (`accessibilityIdentifier`) are key for stable tests.
Debugging with LLDB: LLDB is the Xcode debugger. Commands: `po` (print object), `p` (print value), `expr` (evaluate expression), `bt` (backtrace), `frame variable`, `image lookup`. Use `breakpoint set` / `br s`. Watchpoints monitor variable changes. `lldbinit` can customize the debugger.
Instruments & Profiling: Xcode Instruments profiles performance. Templates: Time Profiler (CPU), Allocations (memory), Leaks (retain cycles), Network, Core Data, Animation Hitches. The debug navigator provides quick access to energy, memory, CPU logs. `os_signpost` marks custom instrumentation points.
TestFlight & Crashlytics: TestFlight distributes pre-release builds to testers via App Store Connect. Xcode archives upload to TestFlight. Crashlytics (Firebase) provides real-time crash reporting with stack traces and breadcrumbs. Use `Crashlytics.crashlytics().record()` for non-fatal errors. `setCustomValue` adds context to crash reports.

Certificates & Provisioning: Apple Developer Program membership is required for distribution. Certificates: Development (run on device), Distribution (App Store, Ad-Hoc). Provisioning Profiles combine certificate + App ID + devices. Xcode manages signing automatically with `Automatically manage signing`. Manual signing requires Apple Developer Portal access.

# Certificate types:
# iOS Development — run on registered devices
# iOS Distribution — App Store and Ad-Hoc
# Apple Push Services — push notifications
# Pass Type ID — Apple Wallet

# Provisioning Profile contains:
# - Certificate (private key on your Mac)
# - App ID (bundle identifier + capabilities)
# - Device IDs (for Development/Ad-Hoc)

# Xcode managed (recommended)
# Signing & Capabilities > Automatically manage signing
# Xcode generates certificates and profiles automatically

# Distribution methods:
# - App Store: public release via App Store
# - Ad-Hoc: limited devices (up to 100 per year)
# - Enterprise: in-house apps (requires Enterprise account)
# - Development: up to 100 registered devices
App Store Connect: App Store Connect manages app listing, pricing, in-app purchases, TestFlight, and analytics. App Information includes name, subtitle, privacy policy, categories. Version Release: manual or automatic. Screenshots (6.7", 6.5", 5.5", iPad) are required. `xcodebuild` can upload via CLI or Xcode Organizer.

# App Store Connect metadata
# - App Name: up to 30 characters
# - Subtitle: up to 30 characters
# - Privacy Policy URL (required for apps with data collection)
# - Age Rating: 4+ (no objectionable), 9+, 12+, 17+
# - Keywords: 100 characters max, comma-separated

# Pricing
# - Free or paid (tiered pricing: $0.99 - $999.99)
# - In-App Purchases: consumable, non-consumable, auto-renewable subscription, non-renewing subscription

# Upload from command line
$ xcodebuild -workspace App.xcworkspace -scheme "App Release" -archivePath App.xcarchive archive
$ xcodebuild -exportArchive -exportOptionsPlist export.plist -archivePath App.xcarchive -exportPath ./
$ xcrun altool --upload-app -f App.ipa -u username -p app-specific-password
App Review Guidelines: Apple's App Review Guidelines cover safety, performance, business, design, and legal. Key requirements: complete functionality (no placeholder apps), accurate metadata, privacy (nutrition labels, tracking transparency), no hidden features, user-generated content moderation, and subscription transparency.
In-App Purchases & Subscriptions: StoreKit handles in-app purchases and subscriptions. Products created in App Store Connect. `StoreKit 2` (iOS 15+) provides Swift-native APIs with `Product`, `Transaction`, `Entitlement`. `StoreKit 1` uses `SKProductsRequest`, `SKPaymentQueue`. Subscriptions use `SubscriptionStoreView` for management UI.
App Analytics & Metrics: Apple provides App Analytics in App Store Connect: impressions, product page views, downloads, crashes, retention, and engagement. `SKAdNetwork` tracks ad campaign attribution. `AdServices` provides organic attribution. Use `os_log` for structured logging. MetricKit delivers daily performance metrics.
